lessons.title: Definition and core of special structures
lessons.meta: Changing order, omission or focus on a basic skeleton for a communicative purpose
examples: Open the door.
Never have I seen such a view.
It was Mia who solved the problem.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Open still governs the object the door; the imperative omits subject you for a directive purpose.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: The neutral order is I have never seen such a view; fronting Never moves have before I.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: The neutral Mia solved the problem becomes an It-cleft; Mia remains the agent but receives stronger focus.

rules: A special structure is not a new basic pattern; it reshapes an existing clause skeleton.
Marked order normally has a trigger; first restore neutral order, then identify the effect of fronting or inversion.
An emphasis structure keeps participant relations but marks one element as information focus.

questions.question: What neutral subject-predicate relation underlies “Open the door”?
questions.correct: The imperative omits the normally unspoken subject you.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The imperative omits the normally unspoken subject you.

questions.question: What neutral order underlies “Never have I seen...”?
questions.correct: Fronted Never triggers auxiliary-subject inversion.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Fronted Never triggers auxiliary-subject inversion.

questions.question: What is focused in “It was Mia who solved the problem”?
questions.correct: It was...who places focus on Mia.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It was...who places focus on Mia.

narration.text:
同一个意思，可以平平地说，也可以根据当时的目的，把某些词移到前面、把大家都知道的内容省掉，或者把最想强调的部分专门打亮。句子看起来变特别了，但里面“谁做什么”的基本关系通常还在。这些为表达目的改过造型的句子，就是特殊句式。<#0.8#>
Open the door。<#0.8#>这句表面上没有“谁”，可说话人正对着听话人发出指令，执行者就是正在听的人。主语被省掉后，指令更干脆；open 和 the door 的关系没有改变。这种直接要求别人行动的句子，叫祈使句。<#0.9#>
Never have I seen such a view。<#0.8#>Never 被提到最前面，have 也移动到 I 前面，句子用不普通的顺序突出“从来没有”。这种变化叫部分倒装，但看风景的人仍然是 I。<#0.9#>
It was Mia who solved the problem。<#0.8#>说话人特别想指出“是 Mia，不是别人”，于是用 It was 和 who 把 Mia 框在聚光灯下。这叫分裂强调句。无论怎样强调，解题的人仍是 Mia，problem 仍是 solved 指向的对象。
遇到陌生句式，先别猜名称。第一步，找到动词和它对应的主语；第二步，把省掉的内容补回来，再尝试恢复普通陈述顺序；第三步，看它是在发命令、提问，还是突出某个重点。能还原，就能看懂大部分特殊句式。

lessons.title: Affirmative imperatives
lessons.meta: Begin with a base verb; subject you is normally unspoken
examples: Open the window.
Please sit down.
Do come in.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: From You open the window, omit the normally unspoken you and keep the base verb.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Adding please to Sit down changes politeness, not the imperative structure.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Add do before Come in for emphasis; the following verb remains in the base form.

rules: An affirmative imperative normally begins with a base verb and omits subject you.
Add please initially or finally for a polite request; final please is commonly preceded by a comma.
Do before the verb strengthens an affirmative imperative, often for warm invitation or strong urging.

questions.question: Choose the correct imperative.
questions.correct: An imperative uses base-form Open.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: An imperative uses base-form Open.

questions.question: Which is a polite request?
questions.correct: Please can introduce an imperative politely.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Please can introduce an imperative politely.

questions.question: What does do do in “Do come in”?
questions.correct: do adds emphasis in an affirmative imperative.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: do adds emphasis in an affirmative imperative.

lessons.title: Negative imperatives
lessons.meta: Put Don’t or Never before the base verb
examples: Don't touch that wire.
Don't be late.
Never give up.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Negate Touch that wire by adding Don’t before base-form touch.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Negate Be late by putting Don’t before be.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Replace Don’t with Never to strengthen the negative urging.

rules: A normal negative imperative uses Don’t + base verb.
Negative be imperatives also use Don’t be, not normally be not.
Never + base verb means “not ever” and is stronger than Don’t.

questions.question: Choose the correct negative command.
questions.correct: Use Don’t + base verb.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Use Don’t + base verb.

questions.question: How do you say “Do not be late”?
questions.correct: Use Don’t before be as well.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Use Don’t before be as well.

questions.question: How strong is “Never give up”?
questions.correct: Never means not at any time.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Never means not at any time.

lessons.title: Imperatives with let
lessons.meta: Let’s, Let us and Let + object
examples: Let's start.
Let's not argue.
Let him explain.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: We should start can become Let’s start, marking an inclusive suggestion initially.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: To negate Let’s argue, place not between Let’s and the base verb.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: He may explain can become Let him explain; him is object and explain states his action.

rules: Let’s + base verb suggests that speaker and listener act together.
The usual negative of Let’s is Let’s not + base verb.
Let + object + base verb permits, directs or proposes another person’s action.

questions.question: What means “Shall we start”?
questions.correct: Let’s takes a base verb.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Let’s takes a base verb.

questions.question: Choose “Let us not argue.”
questions.correct: Let’s not is the standard common structure.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Let’s not is the standard common structure.

questions.question: Let him ___ .
questions.correct: Use a bare infinitive after the object of let.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Use a bare infinitive after the object of let.

lessons.title: Exclamations with what
lessons.meta: What focuses a noun phrase
examples: What a beautiful day it is!
What useful books these are!
What bad weather we have!

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: From It is a beautiful day, front a beautiful day after what.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Front useful books from These are useful books after what.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Transform The weather is bad by placing noun focus bad weather after what.

rules: Use What + a/an + adjective + singular count noun (+ subject and verb).
Use What + adjective + plural count noun (+ subject and verb), without a/an.
Use What + adjective + uncountable noun (+ subject and verb), without a/an.

questions.question: ___ beautiful day it is!
questions.correct: day is a singular count noun, so use What a.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: day is a singular count noun, so use What a.

questions.question: ___ useful books these are!
questions.correct: books is plural, so omit a.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: books is plural, so omit a.

questions.question: ___ bad weather!
questions.correct: weather is uncountable, so do not use a.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: weather is uncountable, so do not use a.

lessons.title: Exclamations with how
lessons.meta: How focuses an adjective, adverb or predicate degree
examples: How kind she is!
How quickly he runs!
How I miss you!

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: From She is kind, front kind after how while retaining statement order she is.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Front quickly after how from He runs quickly; he runs is not inverted.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: How I miss you! turns the degree in I miss you very much into exclamative focus.

rules: How + adjective + subject + linking verb emphasizes a quality of the subject.
How + adverb + subject + verb emphasizes manner or degree.
How + subject + predicate can emphasize degree, as in How I wish....

questions.question: ___ kind she is!
questions.correct: The focus is adjective kind, so use How.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The focus is adjective kind, so use How.

questions.question: ___ quickly he runs!
questions.correct: quickly is an adverb, so use How.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: quickly is an adverb, so use How.

questions.question: What does “How I miss you!” emphasize?
questions.correct: This is exclamative, not an interrogative how-clause.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: This is exclamative, not an interrogative how-clause.

lessons.title: Yes-no questions
lessons.meta: Move an auxiliary or linking verb before the subject
examples: Is Mia ready?
Can she swim?
Did Tom leave early?

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Mia is ready becomes Is Mia ready?; ready stays in place.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: She can swim becomes Can she swim? by fronting modal can.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Tom left early becomes Did Tom leave early?; tense shifts from left to did.

rules: When be is the predicate, move it before the subject for a yes-no question.
With auxiliaries or modals, move the first auxiliary or modal before the subject.
A lexical verb in present or past simple requires do/does/did, and the lexical verb returns to base form.

questions.question: What is the question form of “Mia is ready”?
questions.correct: Move is directly before Mia.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Move is directly before Mia.

questions.question: What is the question form of “She can swim”?
questions.correct: Front can itself; do not add does.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Front can itself; do not add does.

questions.question: What is the question form of “Tom left early”?
questions.correct: did carries past tense, so left returns to leave.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: did carries past tense, so left returns to leave.

lessons.title: Wh-questions
lessons.meta: Identify the questioned element before deciding on inversion
examples: Where does she live?
Who broke the glass?
I do not know what to say.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Replace the place with where and add do-support: Where does she live?

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Replace subject someone with who: Who broke the glass?

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: What should I say? can be compressed into the wh-infinitive what to say after know.

rules: When the wh-word is not the subject, use wh-word + yes-no question order.
When the wh-word itself is subject, retain statement order and do not add do/does/did.
Wh-word + infinitive expresses an unresolved choice and is not an inverted full wh-question.

questions.question: How do you ask about the place in “She lives in Shanghai”?
questions.correct: Use does + subject + base verb after where.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Use does + subject + base verb after where.

questions.question: Which is correct?
questions.correct: who is the subject, so did is unnecessary.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: who is the subject, so did is unnecessary.

questions.question: What is “what to say” in the sentence?
questions.correct: It functions as the object of know.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It functions as the object of know.

lessons.title: Alternative questions
lessons.meta: Coordinate alternatives with or and answer with a specific choice
examples: Do you want tea or coffee?
Would you like rice or noodles?
Will you stay here or go home?

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Add or coffee to Do you want tea? to form an alternative question.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Adding a second option changes the expected answer from yes/no to the chosen item.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Add the parallel predicate alternative or go home to Will you stay here?

rules: An alternative question coordinates choices with or inside a yes-no question frame.
An alternative question normally requires one alternative, not yes/no.
or can coordinate alternatives of different sizes, but the two alternatives must be grammatically parallel.

questions.question: How do you ask someone to choose a drink?

options.text: Do you want tea or coffee?

questions.correct: or connects the two alternatives.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: or connects the two alternatives.

questions.question: What is the best answer to “Rice or noodles”?
questions.correct: Answer an alternative question with a specific option.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Answer an alternative question with a specific option.

questions.question: Which alternatives are structurally parallel?
questions.correct: Both sides of or are base-verb phrases.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Both sides of or are base-verb phrases.

lessons.title: Tag questions: foundations
lessons.meta: Positive-negative polarity and matching auxiliary and subject
examples: Mia is ready, isn't she?
They cannot swim, can they?
Tom left early, didn't he?

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Add isn’t she? to Mia is ready, matching is and replacing Mia with she.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Add can they? to They can’t swim, retaining modal can.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Add didn’t he? to Tom left early; did carries past tense.

rules: A positive statement normally takes a negative tag.
A negative statement normally takes a positive tag.
If the statement has no be, auxiliary or modal, use do/does/did in the tag.

questions.question: Mia is ready, ___?
questions.correct: The statement is positive, so the tag is negative.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The statement is positive, so the tag is negative.

questions.question: They can't swim, ___?
questions.correct: The statement is negative, so the tag is positive.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The statement is negative, so the tag is positive.

questions.question: Tom left early, ___?
questions.correct: left is a past-simple lexical verb, so use did.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: left is a past-simple lexical verb, so use did.

lessons.title: Foundations of inversion
lessons.meta: Partial and full inversion are different structures
examples: Never have I seen this.
On the hill stands a tower.
Only then did Tom understand the rule.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I have never seen this becomes Never have I seen this; only have inverts after fronted never.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: A tower stands on the hill becomes On the hill stands a tower, with location first and full predicate before subject.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Tom understood the rule only then becomes Only then did Tom understand the rule; constituent roles remain unchanged.

rules: Partial inversion moves only be, an auxiliary or a modal before the subject; the lexical verb stays after it.
Full inversion places the whole predicate before the subject, often in locative, directional or presentational scenes.
Inversion changes surface order but not underlying roles such as subject and object.

questions.question: What inversion is used in “Never have I seen this”?
questions.correct: Only auxiliary have moves before the subject.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Only auxiliary have moves before the subject.

questions.question: What is the subject in “On the hill stands a tower”?
questions.correct: a tower is the subject described by stands.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: a tower is the subject described by stands.

questions.question: What is the object in the inverted sentence?
questions.correct: Inversion does not change the rule as object of understand.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Inversion does not change the rule as object of understand.

lessons.title: Predicate emphasis with do/does/did
lessons.meta: Emphasize that something really is or did happen
examples: I do understand you.
She does care about you.
He did call me.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I understand you becomes I do understand you; understand remains base form.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: She cares about you becomes She does care about you; third-person marking moves to does.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: He called me becomes He did call me; past tense shifts from called to did.

rules: A present-simple affirmative can use do/does + base verb to emphasize truth.
Use does for third-person singular emphasis; the lexical verb no longer takes -s.
Use did + base verb to emphasize a past fact.

questions.question: What does do express in “I do understand you”?
questions.correct: do emphasizes the predicate in an affirmative.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: do emphasizes the predicate in an affirmative.

questions.question: She ___ care about you.
questions.correct: does carries third-person singular, so care is base form.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: does carries third-person singular, so care is base form.

questions.question: Why is call not called in “He did call me”?
questions.correct: Use a base verb after did.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Use a base verb after did.

lessons.title: Ellipsis in coordination
lessons.meta: State shared material once while keeping parallel relations clear
examples: Mia opened the door and walked in.
Tom likes tea, and Amy coffee.
She likes reading and writing.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Omit repeated Mia from Mia opened the door and Mia walked in.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Omit repeated likes from the second coordinated clause.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Share subject and predicate to compress She likes reading and she likes writing.

rules: Coordinated predicates can share one subject, so the second need not repeat it.
A coordinated clause can omit a repeated predicate if it is recoverable exactly.
Ellipsis must not break parallelism or create an impossible shared relation.

questions.question: What is the understood subject of walked?
questions.correct: Both coordinated predicates share Mia.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Both coordinated predicates share Mia.

questions.question: What is omitted before coffee?
questions.correct: The first clause supplies repeated likes.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The first clause supplies repeated likes.

questions.question: Which is parallel?
questions.correct: reading and writing are parallel in form.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: reading and writing are parallel in form.

lessons.title: Nominal substitution with one/ones
lessons.meta: Replace a count noun of the same class, not the identical entity
examples: This pen is old; I need a new one.
The red apples are sweeter than the green ones.
This tea is strong; I prefer milder tea.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: a new pen reduces to a new one, retaining new and replacing pen.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: the green apples reduces to the green ones.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Do not mechanically change milder tea to a milder one because tea is uncountable here.

rules: one substitutes for a previously mentioned singular count noun type.
ones substitutes for plural count nouns and may carry adjectives or determiners.
one/ones does not normally directly substitute for an uncountable noun; omit the noun or use some as appropriate.

questions.question: What does one replace?
questions.correct: one substitutes for singular count noun pen.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: one substitutes for singular count noun pen.

questions.question: What does ones replace?
questions.correct: ones corresponds to plural apples.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: ones corresponds to plural apples.

questions.question: Can uncountable tea be directly replaced by “a mild one”?
questions.correct: one normally substitutes for a singular count noun.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: one normally substitutes for a singular count noun.

groups.title: Advanced · 14 challenge lessons
groups.copy: Handle written inversion, focus restructuring, complex ellipsis and mood boundaries.

lessons.title: Special tag-question matching
lessons.meta: I am, imperatives, Let’s and negative-meaning words
examples: I am late, aren't I?
Let us start, shall we?
He never complains, does he?

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I am late takes the special tag aren’t I?

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Add shall we? to Let’s begin to seek agreement on the joint suggestion.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Though no not appears, never is negative, so add positive does he?

rules: The normal tag after I am is aren’t I.
Imperatives often take will you/won’t you; Let’s normally takes shall we.
With negative-meaning words such as never, hardly, few and little, treat the statement as negative and use a positive tag.

questions.question: I'm late, ___?
questions.correct: The standard common form is aren’t I.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The standard common form is aren’t I.

questions.question: Let's begin, ___?
questions.correct: Let’s is an inclusive suggestion and takes shall we.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Let’s is an inclusive suggestion and takes shall we.

questions.question: He never complains, ___?
questions.correct: never already makes the statement negative in meaning.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: never already makes the statement negative in meaning.

lessons.title: Partial inversion after negative expressions
lessons.meta: Never, seldom, hardly and not until
examples: Seldom does he arrive late.
Not until midnight did they leave.
Hardly had we arrived when it rained.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: He seldom arrives late becomes Seldom does he arrive late with do-support.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: They did not leave until midnight becomes Not until midnight did they leave.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: We had hardly arrived when it rained becomes Hardly had we arrived when it rained.

rules: When never, seldom or rarely begins a clause, use partial inversion.
With initial not until, invert the main clause, not the until-clause.
hardly/scarcely...when and no sooner...than normally invert the past perfect in the first clause.

questions.question: Seldom ___ late.
questions.correct: Initial Seldom triggers does + subject + base verb.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Initial Seldom triggers does + subject + base verb.

questions.question: Not until midnight ___ .
questions.correct: Fronted not until triggers partial inversion in the main clause.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Fronted not until triggers partial inversion in the main clause.

questions.question: Hardly ___ when it rained.
questions.correct: Initial Hardly moves had before the subject.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Initial Hardly moves had before the subject.

lessons.title: Inversion with only, so and neither
lessons.meta: Restrictive adverbials and agreement structures
examples: Only after class did I understand.
Mia can swim, and so can Leo.
Mia cannot swim, and neither can Leo.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I understood only after class becomes Only after class did I understand.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Leo can swim too can be compressed to So can Leo to avoid repeating the predicate.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Leo cannot swim either can be compressed to Neither can Leo.

rules: Initial only + adverbial triggers partial inversion; only modifying the subject does not.
so + auxiliary/modal + subject means another person does too.
neither/nor + auxiliary/modal + subject means another person does not either.

questions.question: Only after class ___ .
questions.correct: Fronted only + time adverbial triggers inversion.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Fronted only + time adverbial triggers inversion.

questions.question: Mia can swim, and ___ Leo.
questions.correct: Retain modal can from the first clause.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Retain modal can from the first clause.

questions.question: Mia cannot swim, and ___ Leo.
questions.correct: neither is negative, so use positive-form can after it.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: neither is negative, so use positive-form can after it.

lessons.title: Full locative and directional inversion
lessons.meta: Set the scene first and postpone the new-information subject
examples: Beside the river stands an old house.
Here comes the bus.
Here he comes.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: An old house stands beside the river becomes Beside the river stands an old house.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: The bus comes here becomes Here comes the bus for live presentation.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Here comes Tom allows a postposed noun subject; with a pronoun use Here he comes.

rules: With a fronted locative and a noun-phrase subject, full inversion may use location + predicate + subject.
Initial here, there, in, out, up or down can present appearance or movement.
With a personal-pronoun subject, these here/there structures normally do not use full inversion.

questions.question: Beside the river ___ .
questions.correct: Full inversion places the predicate before a noun-phrase subject.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Full inversion places the predicate before a noun-phrase subject.

questions.question: Here ___ the bus.
questions.correct: Full inversion directly uses comes + noun subject.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Full inversion directly uses comes + noun subject.

questions.question: Which is correct?
questions.correct: Pronoun subject he normally stays before the predicate.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Pronoun subject he normally stays before the predicate.

lessons.title: It-cleft sentences
lessons.meta: It is/was + focus + that/who...
examples: It was Mia that solved the problem.
It was Tom who called me.
It was yesterday that we met.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Mia solved the problem becomes It was Mia that solved the problem by placing Mia in the focus slot.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Tom called me becomes It was Tom who called me, with who referring to the person focus.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: We met yesterday alternates with It was yesterday that we met, focusing the time adverbial.

rules: It is/was + focused element + that... can emphasize a subject, object or adverbial.
Use who or that for a person; normally use that for a thing or adverbial.
To test a cleft, remove It is/was and that/who and see whether the remainder reconstructs a full clause.

questions.question: What is focused in the sentence?
questions.correct: The focus lies between was and that.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The focus lies between was and that.

questions.question: What can introduce the remaining clause when Tom is focused?
questions.correct: The focus is a person, so who is possible.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The focus is a person, so who is possible.

questions.question: What is the restored sentence?
questions.correct: Remove the cleft frame and return yesterday to its adverbial position.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Remove the cleft frame and return yesterday to its adverbial position.

lessons.title: Wh-cleft sentences
lessons.meta: What... is/was... identifies and contrasts focus
examples: What I need is a rest.
What she wants is to leave early.
All I want is some peace.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I need a rest becomes What I need is a rest, making the original object the focused complement.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: She wants to leave early becomes What she wants is to leave early; the what-clause is not inverted.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I only want some peace can be focused as All I want is some peace.

rules: What-clause + be + focused complement means “the thing that ... is ...”.
The what-clause in a wh-cleft is a nominal subject clause, not a wh-question.
all can introduce a related focusing structure in limited contexts: All I want is....

questions.question: What is the focus?
questions.correct: a rest after be supplies the identified focus.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: a rest after be supplies the identified focus.

questions.question: What is “What she wants” as a whole?
questions.correct: It precedes is and functions as subject.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It precedes is and functions as subject.

questions.question: What is some peace in the sentence?
questions.correct: It follows be and identifies All I want.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It follows be and identifies All I want.

lessons.title: Fronting and information focus
lessons.meta: Place a topic or contrastive element first
examples: This book I really enjoyed.
Very difficult the task was.
Yesterday I met her.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I enjoyed this book becomes This book I enjoyed; I enjoyed is not inverted.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: The task was very difficult becomes Very difficult the task was for strong contrast.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I met her yesterday becomes Yesterday I met her; only the adverbial moves.

rules: Object fronting can establish contrastive topic and normally does not invert subject and verb.
Predicative fronting is literary or strongly contrastive, not neutral everyday order.
Whether fronting triggers inversion depends on the trigger and construction; fronting alone does not always invert.

questions.question: What is the original position of This book?
questions.correct: Restore it as I enjoyed this book.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Restore it as I enjoyed this book.

questions.question: What register is this order?
questions.correct: Neutral order is The task was very difficult.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Neutral order is The task was very difficult.

questions.question: Must it become “Yesterday did I meet her”?
questions.correct: Ordinary initial yesterday does not trigger inversion.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Ordinary initial yesterday does not trigger inversion.

lessons.title: Ellipsis in adverbial clauses
lessons.meta: Omit the subordinate subject and be when subjects are coreferential
examples: When young, he lived abroad.
When crossing the road, you must look both ways.
If necessary, call me.

analyses.label: Time adverbial with he was omitted

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: When he was young becomes When young by omitting coreferential he and be.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: When you are crossing the road can reduce to When crossing the road only when the main subject is also you.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: If it is necessary reduces to If necessary, retaining the conjunction and predicative.

rules: When an adverbial clause shares the main-clause subject and contains be, its subject and be may be omitted.
Do not use this ellipsis when subjects differ, or a dangling element results.
Fixed reductions such as if necessary/possible/any omit it is and should be recognized as units.

questions.question: What is omitted?
questions.correct: The subordinate subject is coreferential with main-clause he.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The subordinate subject is coreferential with main-clause he.

questions.question: What must be the understood subject of crossing?
questions.correct: The understood subordinate subject must match the main subject.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The understood subordinate subject must match the main subject.

questions.question: What can “If necessary” expand to?
questions.correct: The fixed omission is it is.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The fixed omission is it is.

lessons.title: Infinitival ellipsis
lessons.meta: Keep to and omit a recoverable verb phrase
examples: I wanted to go, but I was unable to.
She is not a doctor, but she hopes to be.
Will you join us? I would love to.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I was unable to go reduces to I was unable to, retaining to.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: she hopes to be a doctor reduces to she hopes to be, retaining linking be.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I would love to join you reduces to I would love to because the action is clear from context.

rules: To avoid repetition, an infinitive may retain only to while its verb phrase is recovered from context.
When the omitted verb is be or perfect have, retain be or have when needed to preserve structure.
Ellipsis requires uniquely recoverable content; do not leave bare to without a clear antecedent.

questions.question: What is omitted after to?
questions.correct: The earlier wanted to go supplies go.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The earlier wanted to go supplies go.

questions.question: Why is be retained?
questions.correct: Only repeated predicative a doctor is omitted.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: Only repeated predicative a doctor is omitted.

questions.question: Where is the omitted content recovered from?
questions.correct: The question supplies join us.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The question supplies join us.

lessons.title: Substitution with do, so and not
lessons.meta: Replace a predicate or a whole proposition
examples: Mia reads more than I do.
Will it rain? I think so.
Will it rain? I hope not.

analyses.label: so substituting for a positive clause
not substituting for a negative clause

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Mia reads more than I read becomes Mia reads more than I do.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I think that it will rain reduces to I think so.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I hope that it will not rain reduces to I hope not.

rules: do/does/did can substitute for a lexical-verb predicate and inflect for subject and tense.
After think, hope, suppose and believe, so can substitute for a positive proposition.
With suitable verbs such as hope, suppose and believe, not can substitute for a negative proposition, but the pattern is lexically restricted.

questions.question: What does do replace?
questions.correct: do avoids repeating predicate read.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: do avoids repeating predicate read.

questions.question: What can so replace?
questions.correct: so substitutes for the whole positive proposition.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: so substitutes for the whole positive proposition.

questions.question: What does “I hope not” mean?

options.text: I hope it will not rain.

questions.correct: not substitutes for the negative proposition it will not rain.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: not substitutes for the negative proposition it will not rain.

lessons.title: Parentheticals and the clause skeleton
lessons.meta: Added comments do not fill core clause roles
examples: The plan, I think, will work.
Mia— as you know— is reliable.
Your answer, in my opinion, is correct.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I think the plan will work can reposition I think parenthetically: The plan, I think, will work.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Insert as you know into Mia is reliable and mark its boundaries with paired punctuation.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Add in my opinion to Your answer is correct to mark viewpoint; the skeleton stays unchanged.

rules: A parenthetical gives stance, source or discourse organization and can normally be removed without damaging the core clause.
Commas, dashes or parentheses can set off a parenthetical, with punctuation matching the interruption strength.
Do not mistake a parenthetical for the main predicate; temporarily remove it to find the skeleton.

questions.question: What is the core after removing I think?
questions.correct: I think is a parenthetical comment.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: I think is a parenthetical comment.

questions.question: What do the dashes around as you know mark?
questions.correct: The dashes set off an added comment.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The dashes set off an added comment.

questions.question: What is the subject-predicate skeleton?
questions.correct: in my opinion is outside the core skeleton.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: in my opinion is outside the core skeleton.

lessons.title: wish and unreal wishes
lessons.meta: Past forms mark present distance; past perfect marks past regret
examples: I wish I knew the answer.
She wishes she had studied harder.
I wish you would be quiet.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I do not know the answer becomes I wish I knew the answer, using past form for present unreality.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: She did not study hard enough becomes She wishes she had studied harder.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Please be quiet can become I wish you would be quiet, adding sustained expectation or annoyance.

rules: wish + past-form clause can express a wish contrary to the present.
wish + had + past participle expresses regret about a completed past fact.
wish + would often asks another person or situation to change and may convey annoyance or expectation; it is not the normal form for one’s own controllable action.

questions.question: What does the sentence imply?
questions.correct: knew marks distance from present reality.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: knew marks distance from present reality.

questions.question: What does it express?

options.text: Regret that she did not study harder

questions.correct: had studied refers to an unrealized past alternative.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: had studied refers to an unrealized past alternative.

questions.question: What does it express?

options.text: A wish for the other person to change

questions.correct: would points to a desired change.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: would points to a desired change.

lessons.title: Suggestion, demand and necessity structures
lessons.meta: The school-level boundary of suggest that... (should) do
examples: They suggested that he (should) rest.
It is essential that everyone (should) attend.
The evidence suggests that he is right.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: He should rest can be embedded as They suggested that he (should) rest.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: Everyone should attend can become It is essential that everyone (should) attend.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: shows can become suggests in The evidence shows that he is right, without triggering a mandative base form.

rules: After verbs of suggestion or demand such as suggest, demand, insist and recommend, the that-clause may use (should) + base verb.
It is important/necessary/essential that... may use (should) + base verb for necessity.
When suggest means “indicate”, it is not mandative; its clause uses ordinary tense for a fact.

questions.question: They suggested that he ___ .
questions.correct: A mandative clause uses the base verb; should may be omitted.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: A mandative clause uses the base verb; should may be omitted.

questions.question: It is essential that everyone ___ .
questions.correct: The necessity construction may use base-form attend.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The necessity construction may use base-form attend.

questions.question: The evidence suggests that he ___ right.
questions.correct: suggests means “indicates”, so use ordinary tense.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: suggests means “indicates”, so use ordinary tense.

lessons.title: Integrated special-structure analysis
lessons.meta: Restore neutral order before identifying inversion, emphasis, ellipsis or substitution
examples: How kind she is!
It was only then that I understood.
Mia chose the red pen, and Leo the blue one.

analyses.label: one substitutes for pen; chose is omitted

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: She is very kind becomes How kind she is!; How is she? instead inverts is for interrogation.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: I understood only then can become either Only then did I understand or It was only then that I understood.

exampleNotes.title: Structure transformation
exampleNotes.body: ...Leo chose the blue pen reduces to ...Leo the blue one through predicate ellipsis and noun substitution.

rules: Distinguish exclamative fronting from interrogative inversion: How kind she is! keeps statement order, while How is she? is a question.
Distinguish inversion after fronted only from It-cleft emphasis: both can focus an adverbial but use different frames.
Both ellipsis and substitution avoid repetition; ellipsis leaves material unspoken, while substitution inserts forms such as one, do or so.

questions.question: Which is an exclamation?
questions.correct: The exclamation retains statement order she is.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: The exclamation retains statement order she is.

questions.question: What structure is this?
questions.correct: It was...that is a cleft frame.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: It was...that is a cleft frame.

questions.question: What does the sentence contain?

options.text: one substitutes for pen and chose is omitted

questions.correct: one is a substitute and chose can be restored after Leo.
questions.wrong: Check the rule: one is a substitute and chose can be restored after Leo.
